title: Piano Trio in B-flat major, “Archduke”
hook: Beethoven’s broadest trio, and the piece he played at his last public concert as a pianist.

painting.title: Caspar David Friedrich in His Studio
painting.pairingNote: Painted in 1811, the year Beethoven finished the trio; an artist alone in a bare, quiet room, wholly absorbed in his work, with the same unhurried calm as the trio’s opening theme and its hymn-like slow movement.

facts: Beethoven sketched the trio in 1810 and finished it in March 1811. He dedicated it to Archduke Rudolph of Austria, the Emperor’s youngest brother, who was his piano and composition pupil, his friend and one of his most faithful patrons. Beethoven dedicated more than a dozen works to him, among them the *Emperor* Concerto and the *Missa solemnis*. The nickname comes from that dedication.

The first public performance took place on 11 April 1814 at the Viennese hotel Zum römischen Kaiser, with Beethoven at the piano, Ignaz Schuppanzigh (violin) and Joseph Linke (cello). By then he was very deaf. The violinist Louis Spohr, at a rehearsal, wrote that in loud passages he pounded until the strings jangled, and in soft ones whole groups of notes went missing. After a repeat a few weeks later, Beethoven never played in public as a pianist again.

It is long and spacious: more than forty minutes, with the piano a full partner and often the leader rather than an accompanist. The scherzo comes second and the slow movement third, the reverse of the usual order, and the slow movement runs straight into the finale without a break.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a broad, singing opening (I), a sly scherzo with a creeping trio (II), a hymn and variations (III), a lively, rustic rondo (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: The piano alone sings a broad, noble tune; the violin and cello take it up. The movement is a [[sonata-form|sonata form]] that seems in no hurry. Its most magical passage comes at the end of the [[development|development]], when the strings pluck and the piano trills, almost in a whisper.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a calm, warm melody in the piano, moving in even steps, like a slow march for strings.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a lighter, rising tune in an unexpected, brighter key, G major.

stops.hear: The piano alone plays a broad, singing tune in chords
The violin and cello take over the tune; the piano answers with flowing figures
A brighter tune, lifting upwards, in a new key
stops.happening: Theme 2, in G major rather than the expected F major

stops.hear: The broad opening tune again in the piano
The opening tune is taken apart; short pieces of it move through new keys
Very quiet: the violin and cello pluck single notes while the piano trills softly; the tune is barely there
The broad tune returns, the strings still half-whispering around it
The music lingers and widens; the main tune comes back strongly

notice: Listen to who has the tune. The piano starts, but within a minute all three are sharing it, and the cello often sings in its high, tenor register.
Notice how quiet the end of the development gets. Plucked strings and trills replace the melody altogether for a while.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Kempff, Szeryng and Fournier recorded the trio in Vevey, Switzerland, in April 1970, during their complete set of Beethoven’s piano trios for Deutsche Grammophon. They take the first movement’s repeat (≈ 3:15). On the Spotify album, a collection of Beethoven’s trios, it is tracks 20–23.

movements.heading: Scherzo. Allegro
movements.summary: A light, mischievous [[scherzo|scherzo]] that begins with the cello alone, climbing a scale. The middle section, the [[trio|trio]], is strange and shadowy: a slow, chromatic, creeping tune that the instruments take up one after another, broken by a loud, swinging waltz. Beethoven writes out the plan in full: scherzo, trio, scherzo, trio, scherzo, then a short [[coda|coda]].

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: a rising scale in the cello, answered by the violin, with a skipping, dance-like tune.

mainIdeas.name: The trio, part 1
mainIdeas.description: a winding, chromatic line in a low register, in B-flat minor, built as a [[fugato|fugato]].

mainIdeas.name: The trio, part 2
mainIdeas.description: a loud, cheerful waltz in the piano.

stops.hear: The cello alone climbs a quiet scale; the violin answers; then a skipping tune
The light disappears: the cello starts a slow, winding, chromatic line low down, and the others follow one by one
stops.happening: The trio, a [[fugato|fugato]] in B-flat minor

stops.hear: A sudden loud, swinging waltz in the piano
stops.happening: The second idea of the trio

stops.hear: The cello’s rising scale and the skipping tune again
The creeping chromatic line and the waltz, a second time
stops.happening: The trio again, as Beethoven wrote it

stops.hear: The scherzo for the third time

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The creeping line slips in once more, then a quick, abrupt ending

notice: Listen for the cello at the start. Beginning a scherzo with a single, quiet low instrument playing a scale is a joke on the listener: it sounds like a warm-up.
In the trio, follow the creeping line from instrument to instrument. It moves by the smallest steps on the keyboard, which is what makes it sound uneasy.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The scherzo lasts twelve minutes here because Kempff, Szeryng and Fournier play every repeat Beethoven wrote, including the second trio. Some recordings are much shorter: Ashkenazy, Perlman and Harrell take about six and a half minutes.

movements.heading: Andante cantabile ma però con moto
movements.tempo: Andante cantabile ma però con moto
movements.summary: A slow, hymn-like theme in D major, followed by four [[variation|variation]]s in which the notes move faster each time, while the harmony stays the same. Then the music slows, the theme seems to lose its way, and a long, hesitant [[coda|coda]] leads without a break into the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a calm, prayer-like melody in chords, first in the piano, then in the strings.

mainIdeas.name: The variations
mainIdeas.description: the same harmony with ever quicker notes: triplets, then flowing semiquavers, then a shimmering rush, then a return to the theme’s calm.

stops.hear: A slow, solemn melody in chords in the piano; the violin and cello answer with the same music
The piano breaks the tune into flowing notes in threes
Quicker again: the notes run in even, flowing groups
A shimmering rush of very fast notes, the busiest moment of the movement
The rush calms; the theme returns, close to its first shape
The music slows further, drifts into distant keys and keeps stopping, as if it cannot find an ending

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A quiet hesitation, then the finale starts with no pause

notice: Hum the theme’s first notes and keep them in mind. Each variation runs faster on top, but underneath the same slow chords pass by at the same pace.
At the end, notice that there is no gap: the finale begins on the edge of the slow music’s last chord.

movements.heading: Finale. Allegro moderato – Presto
movements.summary: After the hush, a jaunty, slightly lopsided tune bursts in. The finale is a [[rondo|rondo]]: the tune keeps returning between other episodes. At the end the tempo jumps to a fast *Presto* in 6/8 that strays into far-off keys before racing home.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo tune
mainIdeas.description: a cheerful, bouncing melody in the piano, with accents that fall slightly off the beat.

mainIdeas.name: The *Presto*
mainIdeas.description: a quick, skipping version of the tune in groups of three.

stops.hear: A cheerful, bouncing tune in the piano, its accents tripping over the beat
stops.happening: The rondo theme, in B-flat major

stops.hear: A new, more flowing idea passed between the strings
The bouncing tune again
The music wanders through new keys, the tune broken into pieces
The bouncing tune once more, at home
The tempo leaps forward: a fast, skipping dance in threes that slips into distant keys

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The dance whirls home to B-flat and stops with loud chords

notice: Listen to the accents in the rondo tune. They land a little early or late, which gives it its rustic, stumbling swing.

threads.title: Three equals
threads.body: The piano leads but does not dominate. The cello sings high and alone, the violin carries tunes, and the famous passages, the pizzicato in the first movement and the creeping trio, need all three.

threads.title: Calm
threads.body: Two of the four movements are slow or broad, and the slow movement sits third. The weight of the trio lies in its quiet music.

threads.title: Beethoven’s farewell as a pianist
threads.body: He gave the first public performance himself in 1814, already very deaf. It was among his last appearances at the keyboard.
